episodes.title: Are Rappers the GOP’s Shortcut to Black Voters?
cards: Bakari Sellers and Angela Rye open with Crystal Mason, the Black Texas woman acquitted after a roughly 10-year fight over a 2016 provisional ballot that was never counted. Rye also blasts the White House for rescinding more than $800 million in funds Congress approved, including $567 million from Health and Human Services.

The hosts debate the NFL threatening Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair over the names of Palestinian children on his eye tape. Rye says players and owners should stand with him; Sellers asks how much one athlete should be expected to sacrifice.

Metro Atlanta leads the nation in evictions, and Black renters face about 70% of cases while making up 52% of renters. Rye praises California's AB 1661, which sends $5,000 payments from oil-well penalties to families in historically Black Los Angeles neighborhoods near drilling sites.

With 33 days until the midterms, Sellers walks through the Senate toss-ups. Both hosts criticize Black Republicans John James and Byron Donalds, and Rye recalls being told as a young staffer that the Republican line is shorter but brings the wrong kind of attention.

quotes.text: What I would expect is that players and owners would rally behind him because, you know, survival is not political.
quotes.speaker: Angela Rye
quotes.context: The hosts are debating whether a Houston Texans linebacker should keep writing the names of Palestinian children on his eye tape after the NFL threatened to bar him from playing.

quotes.text: I think it has a lot to do with the fact that there are people who really want to evict their tenants because property values have gone up.
quotes.context: The hosts are discussing why metro Atlanta leads the country in evictions, where Black residents are 52% of renters but 70% of eviction cases, and where landlords can file quickly and cheaply.

quotes.text: But I do think that this strategy of trying to pick off Black male voters is one that people have to give more credence to.
quotes.context: The hosts have just watched a campaign video of Michigan Republican John James riding around Detroit with a rapper, and are weighing how seriously to take the Republican push for Black male voters.

quotes.text: The line over there is shorter and you'll get attention quicker, but it's not the attention you want.
quotes.speaker: Angela Rye, recalling advice from Gary Flowers
quotes.context: Rye is telling how, as a young Hill staffer, she was offered a six-figure job at J.C. Watts's firm, until her father called Gary Flowers, a former chief of staff to Rev. Jesse Jackson, who gave her this advice.

quotes.text: What Stacey Abrams did, which people don't want to recognize, is it took Stacey over $100 million in nearly a decade to make Georgia blue and people think it's going to happen in a couple of months.
quotes.speaker: Bakari Sellers
quotes.context: Sellers is arguing that changing a state's politics takes years of organizing, pointing to Florida's Republican voter-registration advantage and the long effort behind Georgia's shift.

episodes.takeaway: The hosts argue that Black Republican pitches like John James's Detroit video sound powerful without context, and that Democrats need years of organizing, not months, to flip Southern states.

episodes.title: Should A'ja Wilson Have Been Suspended For Confronting Indiana Fan?
cards: Hill says A'ja Wilson should not have walked toward an Indiana Fever fan who stood, pointed and stepped at her late in game two, even though she understands the frustration. As the league's MVP and its face, Hill argues, Wilson risked her availability and should have had an usher deal with him.

The WNBA gave Wilson a technical but no suspension, ruling she stayed in an area meant for players. Hill calls that the expected outcome: leagues, the NBA included, find a way to keep their best player in a deciding game. She also describes racist abuse and doxxing from people calling themselves Fever or Caitlin Clark fans.

Hill turns to LSU student Kendall Francis, who says a football player raped her. A Title IX process found him responsible, but on appeal he was allowed back on campus and on the team. Hill links the result to Title IX rules rewritten under Betsy DeVos and asks why no one has questioned coach Lane Kiffin.

Hill argues the LSU case drew less attention than Cornell's because Francis is a Black woman. She shares that she and her mother each reported sexual assaults to police decades ago and never heard back, as an example of why many women hesitate to report.
episodes.takeaway: Hill argues the system routinely fails women who report sexual assault, Black women most of all, and Kendall Francis's case at LSU shows it.

quotes.text: If she felt like that fan was out of pocket, tell the usher, make the usher deal with it.
quotes.speaker: Jemele Hill
quotes.context: Hill is explaining why A'ja Wilson should not have confronted the Indiana fan herself, pointing to Russell Westbrook having an abusive fan removed through an usher.

quotes.text: So, the league decided, tell you what, we gonna find every way possible to make sure we do not suspend the best player in the league.
quotes.speaker: Jemele Hill
quotes.context: Hill is explaining why the WNBA chose not to suspend Wilson before a season-deciding game three, ruling she had stayed in an area for players.

quotes.text: She trusted the school to do the right thing. The school did not do the right thing.
quotes.speaker: Jemele Hill
quotes.context: Hill is reacting to LSU student Kendall Francis's account of reporting a rape by a football player who was later allowed back on the team after an appeal.

quotes.text: It's not a money grab, it's a justice grab.
quotes.speaker: Jemele Hill
quotes.context: Hill is explaining why some sexual assault survivors file civil lawsuits, after citing figures showing very few reported assaults end in a prison sentence.

quotes.text: Both of us are still waiting to hear from the police.
quotes.speaker: Jemele Hill
quotes.context: Hill has just described reporting an attempted rape as a child and her mother reporting a rape at gunpoint in 1981, both of which police never followed up on.

headlines.headline: Black UNC Students Say the University Failed Them After a Racist Attack
headlines.summary: A man shouting racial slurs attacked a Black student watch party at UNC-Chapel Hill in August with what students called a makeshift flamethrower, and campus police took nearly 20 minutes to arrive. Black student leaders say the university sent no alert and still hasn't met with them; the attacker got a suspended sentence.

quotes.text: The university and administration, as well as UNC police, have failed to provide clarification as to why the response was delayed, as well as why an emergency alert was not sent out.
quotes.speaker: Sada Maryanov, president of the UNC-Chapel Hill NAACP, quoted by Capital B
quotes.context: Black student leaders are criticizing how UNC and its police handled the Aug. 31 attack on a Black student watch party, including the slow police response and the lack of a campus alert.

quotes.text: We feel that in the recent past there have been many actions that, again, make us feel unsafe and unwanted at a university that we pay tuition dollars to.
quotes.speaker: Samuel Scarborough, Black Student Movement, quoted by Capital B
quotes.context: Scarborough was explaining what Black students want changed on campus, after comparing UNC's response this year with how it handled the Confederate-supporter gathering in 2018.

headlines.headline: A Key Voice for Farmers of Color at USDA Has Gone Silent Under Trump
headlines.summary: The USDA's Advisory Committee on Minority Farmers, the only federal advisory panel that addresses Black farmers, has been frozen since February 2025 and made no recommendations last year. Former members and Rep. Shontel Brown want it restarted; the USDA declined to comment.

quotes.text: If you have no representation, the secretary would never get comments and recommendations from anybody because there’s nobody looking like us sitting on there,
quotes.speaker: Harvey Reed III, former committee chair, quoted by Capital B
quotes.context: Reed, who served on the committee from 2015 to 2023, is explaining why its freeze leaves Black farmers without a voice at the USDA.

quotes.text: The Administration cannot simply ignore a legal mandate because it doesn’t fit its agenda.
quotes.speaker: Rep. Shontel Brown of Ohio, in a statement to Capital B
quotes.context: Brown, vice ranking member on the House Agriculture Committee, was the only lawmaker who answered Capital B's questions about why the committee Congress created has been sidelined.

headlines.headline: At 94, Andrew Young Leads Atlanta Peace Walk With a Message for the World
headlines.summary: Former U.N. ambassador and Atlanta mayor Andrew Young, 94, led an inaugural mile-long peace walk through Atlanta's Rodney Cook Sr. Park, stopping at statues of Martin Luther King Jr., John Lewis and himself to tell stories from the civil rights movement. His foundation plans a peace institute beside the park.

headlines.headline: Throwback Thursday: Megan McArdle Can’t Tell Me Shit About White Supremacy
headlines.summary: Answering a new Megan McArdle column that declares "The Great Awokening" over, Harriot reposts his 2017 reply to her warning against overusing the term "white supremacist." He argues white Americans have never recognized racism while it was happening, so they don't get to decide what counts as white supremacy.

quotes.text: There is only one thing about which I am 100% sure: White people do not get to decide.
quotes.speaker: Michael Harriot
quotes.context: Harriot is weighing whether there are degrees of racism, and says the one thing he is certain of is who should not settle the question.

quotes.text: White people didn’t do a damn thing about the lynch mobs, lunch counters or Jim Crow. We did.
quotes.speaker: Michael Harriot
quotes.context: Harriot is rejecting McArdle's argument that strong language about white supremacy is meant to push white Americans into fighting racism with more urgency.

headlines.headline: The Art of Storytelling, Blacksplained by Ali Siddiq
The President vs. the Press
headlines.summary: Cobb writes that Trump's Sept. 18 order revoking White House access for CNN, Politico and MS NOW fits a long pattern of punishing the press, and a judge Trump appointed has temporarily blocked it. What stands out this time, he argues, is that rival outlets united to back the banned ones.

quotes.text: His behavior cannot be called unexpected at this point. What was noteworthy this time, however, was the way that the press responded.
quotes.speaker: Jelani Cobb
quotes.context: Cobb has just listed Trump's earlier fights with the press, from barring outlets in 2016 to suing several news organizations, before turning to how journalists answered this ban.

headlines.headline: September 30, 2026
headlines.summary: Richardson notes that the last U.S. forces left Iraq this week after more than two decades, and recounts how the 2003 invasion was sold on false claims about weapons of mass destruction. She argues Trump's war on Iran, now in its eighth month, shows the same cowboy mentality.

quotes.text: It later turned out that Powell had not personally vetted the “evidence” he presented and that it was almost entirely either discredited or made up of rumor.
quotes.speaker: Heather Cox Richardson
quotes.context: Richardson is describing Colin Powell's February 2003 speech to the United Nations, which helped win support for invading Iraq.

quotes.text: And yet the United States is entering its eighth month of a war on Iran that Trump apparently began with the same cowboy mentality Bush carried into the war in Iraq.
quotes.speaker: Heather Cox Richardson
quotes.context: Richardson is responding to Trump taking credit on social media for ending the U.S. role in Iraq.

headlines.headline: D.C. Workers Lose Half Their Family Leave as New Laws Take Effect
headlines.summary: Starting Oct. 1, D.C. cut paid leave to care for a seriously ill relative from 12 weeks to six and medical leave from 12 to 10, with a lower $1,100 weekly maximum, through September 2030. Advocates note most workers using these benefits are Black and lower-income.

Van Hollen Bill Would Create Federally Backed Jobs For Long-Term Unemployed Workers
headlines.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen's Ready to Work Act would pay for temporary, paid jobs through local workforce boards for people out of work six months or longer, plus training and help with child care and transportation. Nearly 2 million Americans are long-term unemployed; the bill would also track AI's role in job loss.
